title: Submit a job
intro: A producer creates a job. A queue holds jobs until a worker can execute them. Submission and completion are different events.
takeaway: Accepted means the job entered the queue; it does not mean the requested work has finished.

beats.text: A producer creates a job. A queue holds it until a worker is ready.
Job A enters the queue. The job has been accepted.
A worker takes job A. It leaves the waiting queue.
Execution happens at the worker. Accepted is different from complete.

title: Finish a job
intro: Follow one job from waiting to running to completed. A worker reports completion only after the work succeeds.
takeaway: Waiting, running and completed describe different states. Acknowledgement policy must match the effect being confirmed.

beats.text: Replay job A from its waiting state. No work has happened yet in this replay.
The worker takes job A. Execution starts after it arrives.
The worker executes the job. Leaving the wait queue did not finish it.
The work finishes successfully. Now the job can be marked complete.

title: A backlog grows
intro: A slow worker cannot keep up with incoming jobs. The queue absorbs a short burst, but sustained excess arrivals create a growing backlog.
takeaway: A queue delays overload; it does not create execution capacity. This example has one worker.

beats.text: New scenario: the worker is running A. More jobs arrive while it is busy.
B waits behind the running job. The worker has not taken B.
C arrives before A finishes. C will join B in the queue.
D arrives too. The backlog grows. Arrivals exceed completions here.

title: A full queue pushes back
intro: Give the queue three waiting places. Under this blocking admission policy, submitting E waits at the producer while the queue is full.
takeaway: Backpressure makes upstream production wait or slow. Dropping a job would be a different policy: load shedding.

beats.text: All three waiting places are full. E is still with the producer.
Admission waits at the producer. E does not enter the full queue.
The worker finishes A, then takes B. One waiting place becomes free.
E can now enter the queue. It is accepted, not yet completed.

title: Choose an overload policy
intro: A bounded queue requires an explicit full-queue policy. This lesson illustrates rejection instead of indefinite waiting.
takeaway: Waiting, rejecting and dropping work have different consequences. Expose the outcome rather than calling every submission successful.

beats.text: The queue is full again. This policy rejects new submissions.
The producer asks to submit a job. No waiting place is available.
The queue reports rejection. The producer must handle that result.
The rejected job was not admitted. Make the overload policy explicit.
